title: How's it going? is a greeting, not a question
hook: Nobody actually wants your full life story in the elevator.

sections.heading: The secret code
sections.text: When a coworker says How's it going?, they are not asking for details. The whole exchange is scripted: they say it, you answer fine or not bad, and you ask it back. That is the entire ritual, and it works perfectly.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Newcomers sometimes launch into a real answer about their day, and the other person smiles, nods, and backs away slowly. It is not rude of them — the phrase simply lives in the greeting family, not the question family.

takeaway: Not bad, you? is a complete, perfect answer — always have it ready.
try_it: Today, greet one person with How's it going? and keep your own answer to three words or fewer.

title: Weather is love — the national small talk
hook: Canadians talk about weather the way other cultures ask about family.

sections.heading: The universal topic
sections.text: Weather is the one subject that is safe with absolutely everyone: the stranger at the bus stop, the CEO, the cashier. It has no politics, no risk, and no wrong answer.

sections.heading: The real meaning
sections.text: When a Canadian says Cold enough for you?, they are not sharing meteorology — they are saying I notice you, we are in this together, and I am friendly. Answering warmly is accepting their offer of connection.

takeaway: A comment about the cold or the snow is a small act of belonging — accept it.
try_it: This morning, open one conversation with a comment about today's weather.

title: Sorry is a social lubricant, not an apology
hook: Canadians say sorry when you step on THEIR foot.

sections.heading: The famous reflex
sections.text: In Canada, sorry is used for almost any small collision of life: brushing past someone, reaching for the same item, interrupting by accident. It rarely means I did something wrong — it means I acknowledge this tiny friction and I wish you well.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.text: Use it lightly and often. Saying sorry as you pass someone in a tight aisle costs nothing and makes every interaction smoother. It is not a confession of guilt, so never feel that using it weakens you.

takeaway: A quick sorry in any small collision is polite, not submissive.
try_it: Today, say sorry out loud the next time you bump into anything or anyone, even by a centimetre.

title: Tipping math — 15–20% without panic
hook: The machine will ask you a question with numbers on it. Here is the answer.

sections.heading: The basics
sections.text: At restaurants, tip 15% for okay service, 18% for good service, and 20% when it was great. At coffee shops and takeout counters, tipping is optional — rounding up or skipping is both normal.

sections.heading: The quick math trick
sections.text: Ten percent is easy: move the decimal. Then double it for 20%, or add half of it for 15%. A forty-dollar meal is four dollars at ten percent, so eight at twenty — done before the machine beeps.

takeaway: The tip belongs to the server, not the restaurant — it is how they earn.
try_it: Next time you eat out, calculate the 15% tip out loud in your head before the machine asks.

title: Line-up culture — the sacred queue
hook: The lineup is a Canadian temple, and cutting is the only sin.

sections.heading: The unwritten law
sections.text: Canadians form lines everywhere — coffee, bus, checkout — and the order of arrival is sacred. There are no tokens or ropes; the line just IS, and everyone silently knows their place.

sections.heading: How to belong
sections.text: Stand at the end, keep a polite distance, and never ask to jump ahead unless the situation is genuinely urgent. If you are unsure where the line starts, ask someone: Is the line here? — it is a completely normal question.

takeaway: When in doubt, join the back and ask where the line starts — nobody will mind.
try_it: Today, notice one lineup and consciously give the person ahead of you extra space.

title: We should get coffee sometime — the vague plan
hook: It sounds like a plan. It is actually a compliment.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text: When a new acquaintance says We should get coffee sometime, they are not booking a meeting. They are saying I enjoyed talking to you and I am open to more. Often nothing concrete follows, and that is okay.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.text: The right response is warm and equally vague: That would be great, or Absolutely, I'd love that. If you genuinely want coffee, you can make it real — What does your week look like? — but there is no obligation to push.

takeaway: Treat it as goodwill, not an appointment — and never feel rejected if it never happens.
try_it: Next time someone says it, respond warmly and watch whether they follow up.

title: Workplace small talk — friendly but bounded
hook: Canadians at work are warm, and the warmth has a fence around it.

sections.heading: The friendly fence
sections.text: Weekends, weather, food, sports, and shows are safe at work. Salary, politics, religion, and health details are not — even with people you like. The fence is not coldness; it is how everyone stays comfortable.

sections.heading: Reading the room
sections.text: If someone gives short answers, let them be — they are showing you their preferred distance, and respecting it builds more trust than pushing. Match their energy and the relationship will grow at its own pace.

takeaway: Keep workplace chat light, let others set the depth, and never ask about salary.
try_it: This week, start one workday with a weather or weekend comment to a colleague you rarely talk to.

title: Hockey is civic religion — respect it, don't love it
hook: You do not need to watch a single game. You just need to be polite about it.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Hockey is the closest thing Canada has to a shared civic ritual. Monday mornings, coffee lines, and office kitchens run on quick game talk. You do not need to know the rules to participate — you need one honest sentence.

sections.heading: Your script
sections.text: Did you catch the game last night? can be answered with I didn't see it — how did it go? That asks the other person to talk about something they love, which is the most Canadian-friendly move there is. Nobody will test you on the details.

takeaway: You can be a hockey agnostic and still belong — just ask how the game went.
try_it: This week, ask someone about a game and let them talk for a full minute.

title: Coffee-shop lingo — double-double, regular, dark roast
hook: Ordering coffee in Canada is a language of its own.

sections.heading: The classic words
sections.text: A double-double is a coffee with two creams and two sugars — an icon of Canadian coffee culture. Regular usually means with cream and sugar, and dark roast is simply the type of bean. You can also just say a medium coffee, please, and be perfectly understood.

sections.heading: The ordering rhythm
sections.text: Canadians order like this: size first, then drink, then extras. A medium coffee with one cream, please. Speaking the rhythm feels natural fast, and the person at the counter hears dozens of orders an hour — they will help you through it happily.

takeaway: Size, drink, extras — and double-double is a real, respectable order anywhere in Canada.
try_it: Order a coffee today using exactly the size-first rhythm.

title: The door-hold radius — and the thank-you nod
hook: There is a precise, unspoken distance at which doors must be held.

sections.heading: The rule of doors
sections.text: If someone is within about two metres of a door you are entering, you hold it. Not a grand gesture — just a pause, a held door, and sometimes a smile. Canadians do this automatically and notice when it is done well.

sections.heading: The reply
sections.text: The expected response is a short thanks, and the hold-and-thank exchange often earns an extra smile or a no problem. If someone holds a door for you from far away, a raised hand or a nod is a complete, polite reply.

takeaway: Hold doors within two metres, and always acknowledge the hold with a thanks or a nod.
try_it: Hold a door for a stranger today and count how many thank-yous you collect.

title: Softeners — just, maybe, and no worries
hook: Small words are the secret grammar of Canadian politeness.

sections.heading: The velvet words
sections.text: Canadians wrap requests in softeners to make them feel lighter: Could you just send that over? I was maybe thinking we could... No worries is the all-purpose reply for thank you, sorry, and almost anything small.

sections.heading: Why they matter
sections.text: These words do not change the meaning — they change the feeling. Direct English can sound like an order, while just and maybe make the same request sound like a friendly suggestion. Using them is how you sound warm instead of abrupt.

takeaway: Add just or maybe to your requests, and keep no worries in your back pocket.
try_it: Today, phrase every request you make with a softener, and say no worries at least once.

title: Winter uniform — toque, mitts vs gloves, runners
hook: Winter has a dress code, and Canadians will absolutely tell you about it.

sections.heading: The vocabulary of cold
sections.text: The winter kit is a toque (the knitted hat — never call it a beanie), a scarf, and a warm coat. On your hands: mitts keep fingers together and warmer, while gloves give you dexterity. Runners are what Canadians call running shoes, worn year-round everywhere.

sections.heading: The layer logic
sections.text: Canadians think in layers — a base layer, a sweater, and a shell — because indoor heating is aggressive and outdoor cold is aggressive. Dressing like a local means being able to peel down indoors without melting.

takeaway: Toque on the head, mitts over gloves for warmth, and layers you can shed indoors.
try_it: This week, learn one person's winter trick — everyone has one, and everyone loves being asked.
